r.label: Question 13

oe.title: Which vinegar has the highest concentration of ethanoic acid?
n5: Titration is the most accurate method: pipette a fixed volume (e.g. 20 cm³) of each vinegar into a conical flask, add indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein), and titrate with standard sodium hydroxide from a burette.
Repeat until concordant titres (within 0.2 cm³) are obtained and average them; the vinegar needing the largest titre is the most concentrated.
Calculate the concentration using moles: n = cV and the mole ratio 1:1.
Alternatives: measure pH (lower pH = more H⁺), react with the same mass of a carbonate or magnesium and compare rates or volume of gas, or measure the temperature rise on neutralisation.
Fair test: same volume of each vinegar and same temperature.
higher: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid (only partially ionised), so pH is a poorer comparison than titration, which reacts all of the acid.
Volumetric analysis with a standard solution; dilute strong vinegars accurately with a volumetric flask before titrating.
Calculate % ethanoic acid by mass from the concentration (GFM of CH₃COOH = 60).
diagrams: Labelled titration apparatus: burette (NaOH), pipette, conical flask with vinegar and indicator, white tile.
Results table showing rough and concordant titres.

r.label: Question 10

oe.title: Identifying aluminium, iron, tin and zinc
n5: Use reactivity: react each metal with dilute acid (same concentration, volume and size of strip) and compare the rate of bubbling of hydrogen. Reactivity: Al > Zn > Fe > Sn (Al may look slow at first because of its oxide layer).
Test the gas: hydrogen burns with a pop.
Build cells: pair each metal with copper in an electrolyte and measure the voltage. The further apart in the electrochemical series, the bigger the voltage.
Displacement: a metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt (e.g. zinc in tin(II) sulfate gives a coating of tin).
Other properties: density or magnetism (iron is magnetic); flame tests on the salts formed.
higher: Use reduction potentials / the electrochemical series to predict the cell voltage and the direction of electron flow (from the metal higher in the series).

Measure the rate of hydrogen production quantitatively (gas syringe) and calculate average rates to rank the metals.
eqns: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂;  Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂
Average rate = volume of H₂ / time, e.g. 30 cm³ / 60 s = 0.5 cm³ s⁻¹

r.txt:
5. Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Gold — a very useful metal

Gold has been associated with wealth since before the first gold coins were minted in Lydia (modern Turkey) about 550 BC. It does not react with water, air, alkalis and almost all acids. Gold only has one naturally occurring isotope with mass 197.

As an element it has many uses in the modern world. 1 gram of gold can be beaten into a gold film covering one square metre and thin coatings of gold are used as lubricants in aerospace applications. Gold electroplating can be used to coat electrical connectors and printed circuit boards.

Chemists have recently discovered that gold nanoparticles make superb catalysts for many reactions such as the conversion of alcohols into aldehydes and ketones. It can also be used as a catalyst for removing trace carbon monoxide from gases. In this reaction carbon monoxide reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide.

Gold nanorods can be grown from a dilute solution of auric acid and are used in the treatment of some forms of cancer.

Adapted from Education in Chemistry, Volume 45, November 2008
